 Singapore proposes tougher haze law after Indonesia’s wildfires
 Singapore proposes tougher haze law after Indonesia’s wildfires
 04-Nov-2026, 16:05 04 Nov 2026, 16:05 Bloomberg Share The proposed measures include restrictions on businesses dealing with entities or individuals suspected of contributing to haze-related fires.
 Fires in Indonesia have sent pollution across the region in recent months, pushing air quality in Singapore to ‘very unhealthy’ levels at times. (EPA Images pic) 
 SINGAPORE : Singapore’s government has proposed amendments to toughen its law on cross-border haze, responding to a devastating wildfire season in Indonesia that cloaked the city-state in smog for weeks. 
 Sustainability and environment minister Grace Fu said in Parliament on Wednesday that the country would seek to bolster existing rules with measures including restrictions on businesses dealing with entities or individuals suspected to have engaged in conduct leading to the blazes.
 The changes would also allow for arrests in Singapore and would boost the maximum fines for causing or contributing to haze-related fires from S$100,000 (about US$78,000) per day to US$1 million per day.
 “Following the recent haze episode, it is clear that the status quo is not tenable,” Fu said. 
 “We need better ways to obtain and verify information, trace complex corporate relationships and impose meaningful consequences on errant entities, even where criminal prosecution proves difficult,” Fu added.
 Fires in Indonesia have spewed pollution across the region in recent months, sending air quality to “very unhealthy” levels at times in Singapore. 
 The smog — which has also fueled protests in Indonesia — has spread into Malaysia and the Philippines, closing schools and driving demand for air purifiers.
 The legislation is Singapore’s latest effort to hold firms accountable for the seasonal fires, which are often linked to land clearing for agriculture. 
 The issue has been worsened this year by a strong El Niño that exacerbated and prolonged the dry season. Rains have recently picked up, improving air quality levels.
 Singapore enacted its transboundary haze law in 2014, allowing it to issue daily fines to polluting companies. 
 The city-state tried to enforce that legislation during a severe haze episode in 2015, but conceded at the time it was having difficulty getting information from Indonesian authorities. 
 Several cases remain under investigation.
